metadata.title: Cross Body Ride Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master defensive strategies from Cross Body Ride Bottom in BJJ. Complete guide covering escapes, transitions, and survival tactics with expert insights.

overview:
Cross Body Ride Bottom represents a highly disadvantageous defensive position where the practitioner is on their hands and knees (turtle position) with the opponent mounted across their back in a perpendicular or diagonal orientation. The top player controls from the side, using their bodyweight to flatten the bottom player while threatening back takes, crucifix entries, and various choke attacks. This position requires immediate defensive action as remaining static allows the opponent to systematically break down defenses and advance to more dominant positions.

From the bottom perspective, Cross Body Ride represents a critical juncture where proper defensive framing, hip movement, and explosive timing can create escape opportunities, while poor technique leads to rapid position deterioration. The bottom player must balance survival priorities—protecting the neck, preventing the back take, maintaining base—while actively working toward re-guard or reversal opportunities. Understanding the relationship between upper body frames, hip positioning, and timing is essential for survival and eventual escape from this compromised position.
state_invariants: Bottom player on hands and knees (turtle position) with weight distributed through knees and at least one hand/forearm while defending against top pressure
Top player positioned perpendicular or diagonal across the bottom player's back, with chest/torso making contact with the bottom player's upper back/shoulder area
Bottom player's spine curved defensively with chin tucked to chest, elbows tight to ribs to prevent arm isolation and protect neck from choke attacks
Top player's weight distributed across bottom player's back creating downward and lateral pressure, threatening to flatten the bottom player or advance position
prerequisites: Bottom player has been forced into turtle position from failed guard retention or scramble situation
Top player has established perpendicular or diagonal control across bottom player's back
Bottom player has at least one point of contact with the mat (knees and hands/forearms)
Top player is applying active pressure to prevent bottom player from escaping or standing
key_principles: Maintain defensive posture with chin tucked, elbows tight to ribs, and hands protecting neck to prevent chokes
Keep hips mobile and ready to shift weight to create angles for escape or prevent flattening
Establish strong frames with forearms to create space between your body and opponent's control points
Stay active and constantly working—static defense allows opponent to systematically break you down
Prioritize neck protection above all else, as choke threats are immediate and highly dangerous from this position
Use explosive hip movement and directional changes to disrupt opponent's balance and timing when attempting escapes
Recognize timing windows when opponent shifts weight or adjusts grips to initiate escape sequences

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to flatten or advance to back control
Opponent commits weight forward during back take attempt
Opponent overcommits to one side creating rolling opportunity

decision_tree.condition: If opponent is high on back with hooks threatening but not yet established
If opponent is controlling one arm and attempting crucifix entry
If opponent has heavy cross-body pressure but limited control of arms
If opponent is attempting to flatten you completely to mat

common_errors.error: Remaining static in turtle position without active defensive movement
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to systematically break down defenses and advance to back control or crucifix with minimal resistance
common_errors.correction: Constantly adjust hip position, shift weight, and create small movements to prevent opponent from settling into strong control positions

common_errors.error: Extending arms away from body to post or push against opponent
common_errors.consequence: Arm becomes isolated and vulnerable to crucifix entry, kimura attacks, or opponent uses extended arm as lever to flatten defender
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows tight to ribs with forearms creating frames close to body, only extending arms momentarily during explosive escape attempts

common_errors.error: Lifting head up to look around or assess position
common_errors.consequence: Exposes neck to choke attacks (particularly clock choke, bow and arrow variations) and makes it easier for opponent to control head/neck
common_errors.correction: Maintain chin tucked to chest throughout defensive sequence, using peripheral vision and tactile awareness to track opponent position

common_errors.error: Flattening out to mat in attempt to prevent back take
common_errors.consequence: Eliminates all mobility and escape options, allows opponent to easily establish side control, mount, or pin positions with full weight
common_errors.correction: Maintain some degree of elevation on knees/hands even under heavy pressure, protecting ability to move hips and create escape angles

common_errors.error: Attempting explosive escapes without proper timing or setup
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy on low-percentage escape attempts, potentially worsening position as opponent capitalizes on failed movement
common_errors.correction: Wait for opponent to shift weight or adjust grips before initiating escapes, use small hip adjustments to set up proper angles first

common_errors.error: Ignoring opponent's grip establishment on collar, belt, or arms
common_errors.consequence: Strong grips allow opponent to control movement, prevent escapes, and transition smoothly to more dominant positions
common_errors.correction: Actively fight grips by adjusting posture, using hand fighting, and moving before opponent can consolidate control points

training_drills.name: Granby Roll Escape Repetitions
training_drills.description: From turtle position with partner applying cross-body pressure, practice granby roll escapes to guard recovery. Focus on timing, explosive hip rotation, and protecting neck throughout the roll. Partner provides progressive resistance from 50% to 90% intensity.

training_drills.name: Turtle Survival Under Pressure
training_drills.description: Start in turtle with partner mounted across back attempting to flatten or take back. Defend for timed intervals while maintaining defensive posture, mobile hips, and protected neck. Partner attempts various back attack entries while bottom player works pure survival.

training_drills.name: Escape Sequence Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Chain together multiple escape attempts from cross body ride bottom: attempt granby roll, if blocked transition to hip escape, if blocked attempt technical standup. Partner provides realistic but cooperative resistance, allowing bottom player to flow through entire sequence before resetting.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring from Turtle
training_drills.description: Start in cross body ride bottom position. Bottom player scores points for successful escapes to guard or standing. Top player scores points for back takes, crucifix entries, or submissions. Reset to starting position after each score. Focus on timing, explosive movement, and defensive awareness.

expert_insights.danaher: Cross Body Ride Bottom exemplifies a position where the bottom player's defensive priorities must be perfectly ordered to survive and eventually escape. The systematic approach requires first establishing neck protection through proper chin position and elbow placement, second maintaining hip mobility to prevent complete flattening, and third creating timing windows through small postural adjustments that force the top player to react. The biomechanical reality is that remaining static in this position allows the opponent to methodically break down each defensive layer, while constant micro-adjustments force the opponent to continually re-establish control, creating brief windows where explosive escape techniques like the granby roll become viable. The key insight is that defense in this position is not passive survival but active positional warfare where the bottom player uses frame creation, weight distribution, and timing to transform a highly disadvantageous position into escape opportunities.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: From a competition perspective, Cross Body Ride Bottom is a position you absolutely cannot afford to stay in for extended periods. Top-level competitors will punish static defense by rapidly advancing to back control or crucifix, both of which lead to high-percentage submission threats or dominant point positions. My approach focuses on immediate, explosive escape attempts the moment I recognize the position developing—granby rolls and hip escapes executed with maximum speed and commitment before the opponent can consolidate their control. The mistake most people make is trying to be too defensive and methodical, which plays directly into the top player's hands. You need to create chaos through explosive movement, force scrambles, and be willing to give up some positional control temporarily to avoid the worse outcome of allowing clean back takes. In competition, I'd rather risk a slightly disadvantageous guard position than remain in cross body ride where my opponent has all the initiative.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Cross Body Ride Bottom is one of those positions where creativity and unorthodox movement patterns can really pay off. The traditional granby roll escape is solid, but I've found that incorporating elements from breakdancing and gymnastic movement—like the tactical roll combined with inverted guard entries—can create escape pathways that opponents don't anticipate. The key from a 10th Planet perspective is understanding that your legs are weapons even from turtle, and positions like this can transition into lockdown entries or rubber guard variations if you time the roll correctly and catch their leg during your escape attempt. We also emphasize the psychological aspect—staying calm under heavy pressure, controlling your breathing, and waiting for that perfect moment when your opponent shifts their weight or reaches for a grip. That split-second is when you explode into your escape sequence. The conventional approach treats this purely as a defensive emergency, but I see it as a transition point where unconventional entries to offensive guard systems become possible if you have the right mindset and movement vocabulary.

metadata.title: Cross Body Ride | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Cross Body Ride position in BJJ. Advanced back attack control with 70% back take rate. Complete guide covering harness control, transitions, and submissions.

overview:
Cross Body Ride is an advanced controlling position from turtle where the top practitioner establishes perpendicular chest-to-back contact with the opponent while securing a harness grip (seatbelt control). This position serves as a critical transitional state between turtle top and back control, offering exceptional control and multiple high-percentage paths to dominant positions and submissions. The cross body orientation provides mechanical advantage by directing pressure across the opponent's spine while preventing effective hip escapes.

The position's strategic value lies in its ability to simultaneously immobilize the opponent while creating forcing functions that lead to predictable defensive reactions. When executed properly, Cross Body Ride creates a dilemma where the opponent must choose between defending back exposure or protecting against crucifix entries. This makes it a cornerstone position in modern turtle attack systems, particularly in no-gi grappling where gi-based controls are unavailable.

Mastery of Cross Body Ride requires understanding weight distribution mechanics, maintaining perpendicular alignment, and recognizing the specific defensive reactions that signal transition opportunities. The position is particularly effective against opponents with strong turtle defense, as it bypasses many traditional turtle escape pathways while maintaining offensive initiative.
state_invariants: Top practitioner maintains perpendicular chest-to-back contact with opponent's torso, with ribcage pressing across opponent's spine and shoulder blades, creating crossbody pressure that restricts rotation and forward movement

Harness grip (seatbelt control) is established with one arm over opponent's shoulder and one arm under opponent's armpit, hands clasped together on opponent's far side torso, creating a closed control loop
Bottom practitioner is on hands and knees in defensive turtle posture with head tucked, weight distributed across all four points, attempting to maintain base while defending against back exposure

Top practitioner's hips are positioned alongside opponent's ribs with legs extended or posting for base, weight actively driving down and across opponent's back to prevent them from turning into guard or standing up
Top practitioner maintains perpendicular body alignment to opponent's spine, creating mechanical advantage through crossbody leverage rather than parallel alignment
prerequisites: Opponent in defensive turtle position on hands and knees
Initial harness grip or seatbelt control established
Top practitioner has achieved chest-to-back contact
Ability to maintain perpendicular body alignment to opponent
Understanding of weight distribution to prevent opponent's rotation
key_principles: Maintain perpendicular chest-to-back alignment to maximize pressure across opponent's spine while preventing them from turning to face you
Keep harness grip tight with elbows connected to your own torso, eliminating space that opponent could use to strip grips or create frames
Drive weight downward and forward through your chest into opponent's back, collapsing their turtle structure and forcing them to choose between protecting their back or their arms
Control opponent's far hip with your near leg hook or positioning to prevent them from sitting through to guard or rolling away from pressure
Continuously read opponent's weight shifts and base adjustments to anticipate defensive reactions and time transitions to back control or crucifix
Maintain active pressure and constant threat of advancement rather than static holding, forcing opponent into defensive errors
Use perpendicular leverage to create isolation on opponent's near-side arm when they attempt to base out, setting up crucifix entries

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent posts near arm to prevent back take
Opponent attempts to sit through to guard
Opponent turns into you to defend far side
Opponent extends near arm for posting

decision_tree.condition: If opponent keeps elbows tight and maintains strong turtle base without extending arms
Else if opponent posts near-side arm to base out against crossbody pressure
Else if opponent attempts to sit through toward you or roll away from pressure
Else if opponent turns into you aggressively or tries to swim inside arm free

common_errors.error: Maintaining parallel alignment instead of perpendicular crossbody position
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to turn into you and recover guard, eliminates mechanical advantage of crossbody pressure, makes it easier for opponent to stand or roll away
common_errors.correction: Keep your chest perpendicular to opponent's spine with ribcage pressing across their shoulder blades, actively prevent parallel alignment by maintaining perpendicular hip positioning

common_errors.error: Allowing slack in the harness grip or seatbelt control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can strip grips, create frames, or rotate their torso to escape, reduces control and allows them to defend transitions more effectively
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows tight to your own body with hands clasped firmly on opponent's far side, continuously pull opponent's torso toward you while driving chest pressure down and across their back

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's far hip with leg positioning
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can sit through to guard easily, roll away from pressure, or create angle changes that compromise your control and transition opportunities
common_errors.correction: Hook your near leg around opponent's far hip or post your knee against their hip to prevent rotation, use this control to steer their movement and anticipate defensive reactions

common_errors.error: Using static pressure instead of dynamic weight shifts
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can establish stable base and wait for you to tire, reduces effectiveness of forcing opponent into reactions, makes transitions predictable and easier to defend
common_errors.correction: Constantly shift weight and pressure direction to keep opponent off-balance, use wave-like pressure that alternates between forward drive and crossbody compression to create movement

common_errors.error: Committing too early to back take without establishing proper control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes during transition, you lose dominant position, fall into opponent's guard, or give up advantageous attacking position for lower-percentage scramble
common_errors.correction: Establish secure crossbody ride first with tight harness and hip control, then systematically work toward back exposure by creating reactions through pressure variations

common_errors.error: Neglecting to read opponent's weight distribution and defensive priorities
common_errors.consequence: Miss optimal timing for transitions, force techniques against opponent's strongest defensive posture, waste energy on low-percentage attacks when better options are available
common_errors.correction: Feel opponent's weight shifts through your chest pressure and harness grip, when they post an arm or shift weight to defend one side, immediately attack the exposed area with appropriate transition

training_drills.name: Crossbody Pressure Maintenance Drill
training_drills.description: Partner starts in defensive turtle, you establish cross body ride with harness grip. Partner attempts to maintain base and turn into you while you maintain perpendicular alignment and downward pressure for 2-minute rounds. Focus on weight distribution, grip maintenance, and preventing opponent rotation without attempting transitions.

training_drills.name: Reaction-Based Transition Drill
training_drills.description: From established cross body ride, partner gives specific defensive reactions (posting near arm, sitting through, turning in, standing attempt) one at a time. You must identify the reaction and execute the appropriate counter-transition within 3 seconds. Rotate through all four reactions systematically to develop pattern recognition.

training_drills.name: Harness to Back Take Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Starting from cross body ride, flow between crab ride position and full back control repeatedly while maintaining harness grip throughout. Partner provides 50% resistance, focusing on creating the dilemma between defending back hooks versus protecting arms. Alternate roles every 3 minutes to develop both attacking and defensive feel.

training_drills.name: Crucifix Entry Timing Drill
training_drills.description: Partner in turtle posts near-side arm at various intensities and timings. You must capture the posted arm and establish crucifix control using your legs while maintaining harness grip with your arms. Focus on timing the arm isolation when opponent's weight commits to the post rather than forcing it prematurely.

expert_insights.danaher: Cross Body Ride represents a critical inflection point in the turtle attack sequence where proper mechanical understanding separates functional control from mere positional achievement. The position's efficacy derives from its perpendicular orientation creating what I term 'crossbody leverage' - a force vector that simultaneously restricts opponent rotation while exposing multiple attack vectors. The harness grip functions as a closed control loop that divides opponent's defensive capacity between upper body immobilization and lower body base maintenance. This division creates predictable defensive hierarchies where opponent must prioritize either protecting back exposure or preventing arm isolation. Advanced practitioners recognize that Cross Body Ride is fundamentally a forcing position rather than a resting position - its purpose is to create binary defensive choices that lead to deterministic outcomes. When opponent defends the back take by keeping elbows tight, this very defense creates the posting reaction that enables crucifix entry. Conversely, when opponent prevents crucifix by refusing to post, they expose the pathway to back control. Understanding this mechanical dilemma transforms Cross Body Ride from a transitional nuisance into a systematic attacking platform.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, Cross Body Ride is my preferred entry point for back attacks against elite turtle defense because it immediately puts opponent in a losing position where all their defensive options lead to worse positions. Unlike traditional turtle attacks that often stall against good defense, cross body ride creates continuous advancement pressure that's extremely difficult to neutralize without making critical errors. My approach focuses on establishing the position quickly from any turtle situation, then using heavy crossbody pressure to force opponent's hands - literally. When I drive my chest across their back and pull the harness tight, they have maybe 2-3 seconds before they have to post an arm or turn into me, and either reaction gives me exactly what I want. Against world-class opponents, I've found the key is varying your pressure rhythm - sometimes steady and heavy, sometimes pulsing and dynamic - to prevent them from timing their defensive movements. The position's beauty is that it requires relatively low energy expenditure while forcing opponent to work extremely hard to maintain their turtle structure. I can stay here for 30-40 seconds if needed, systematically breaking down their posture until the back take or crucifix becomes inevitable. It's become such a reliable position in my game that I actively work to put opponents in turtle specifically to access this control.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Cross Body Ride is where the Twister system really starts to come alive, man. Most people think of it as just a step toward back control, but we've weaponized it as a gateway to the whole truck position universe. When you're riding crossbody with that harness grip, you're not just controlling position - you're setting up one of the most devastating submission systems in no-gi grappling. The key innovation in our system is recognizing that when opponent sits through to defend the back take, that's not a defensive success - that's them walking right into the truck entry. We've spent years developing specific pressure variations and grip adjustments that make opponent choose between getting their back taken or sitting into the truck, and both paths lead to serious submission threats. The position also works beautifully with our lockdown game because if you get the cross body ride from half guard situations, you can use similar mechanics. What makes this position so valuable in 10th Planet methodology is how it bypasses traditional gi-based turtle defenses that rely on collar and sleeve grips. In no-gi, once you establish that perpendicular chest pressure with harness control, opponent's defensive options collapse rapidly. We drill specific sequences from cross body to crab ride to twister, making it a systematic progression rather than hoping opponent makes mistakes. The position rewards creativity too - there are so many grip variations and pressure angles you can experiment with while maintaining the core mechanical advantage.

overview:
Cross Body Ride Top is a dominant controlling position used when the opponent is in turtle position. The top practitioner controls the opponent's back from a perpendicular angle, using body weight and strategic grips to prevent escapes while setting up back takes and submissions. This position is characterized by the top player's chest positioned across the opponent's back, with hooks or control points established to prevent the bottom player from either standing up or rolling through.

The Cross Body Ride is a critical transitional position in no-gi grappling and serves as a gateway to back control, the crucifix, and various submission attacks. It allows the top player to apply heavy shoulder pressure while maintaining mobility to follow the opponent's defensive movements. The position is particularly effective because it neutralizes the turtle position's defensive advantages while creating multiple offensive pathways.

Modern approaches to the Cross Body Ride emphasize dynamic control rather than static holding, with practitioners constantly adjusting weight distribution and grip placement based on the opponent's reactions. This position represents the intersection of technical control and athletic adaptability, requiring practitioners to read and respond to defensive movements while maintaining dominant positioning throughout the engagement.
state_invariants: Top player's chest positioned perpendicular across opponent's back, creating heavy cross-body pressure through shoulder and upper torso contact with opponent's spine and shoulder blade area
Opponent in turtle position with knees and hands/elbows on mat, back exposed and facing downward, unable to achieve standing or supine positions
Top player maintains at least one hook (arm or leg) controlling opponent's near side, preventing rotation and escape while serving as anchor point for transitions
Weight distribution directed through shoulder and upper body into opponent's back, collapsing their turtle structure while maintaining top player's base on opposite side
Top player's hips positioned to side and slightly back, allowing mobility to follow opponent's movements while maintaining perpendicular angle of attack
prerequisites: Opponent in defensive turtle position with back exposed
Top player has achieved perpendicular angle relative to opponent's spine
Initial control established via collar tie, overhook, or seatbelt grip
Top player's weight successfully loaded onto opponent's back
Bottom player's forward movement or standing attempts have been neutralized
key_principles: Maintain perpendicular angle with chest across opponent's back to maximize pressure and control options
Keep weight heavy on opponent's shoulders to collapse their turtle structure and limit mobility
Use near-side hook (arm or leg) as primary anchor point while opposite side maintains base and mobility
Stay mobile and ready to follow opponent's rotation, avoiding being rolled through or escaped
Transition decisively when opponent exposes back or extends limbs, capitalizing on defensive reactions
Control opponent's hips and shoulders simultaneously to prevent explosive escapes or position changes
Maintain constant pressure to drain opponent's energy while preserving your own through efficient weight distribution

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to roll forward or granby
Opponent extends near arm to post or defend
Opponent turns into you or attempts to stand
Opponent flattens to belly trying to escape hooks

decision_tree.condition: If opponent stays static in turtle or attempts to hide arms close to body
If opponent attempts forward roll, granby, or explosive rotation
If opponent extends near arm to post or defend neck
If opponent attempts to stand or elevate hips significantly
If opponent flattens completely to belly exposing back

common_errors.error: Staying too static and allowing opponent to build defensive structure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent successfully stalls position or times escape when top player's weight shifts
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant movement and pressure adjustments, never allowing opponent to establish comfortable defensive posture

common_errors.error: Distributing weight too far forward onto opponent's head and neck
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily rolls forward using top player's momentum, escaping to guard or standing position
common_errors.correction: Keep weight centered on opponent's shoulders and upper back, maintaining base with outside leg to prevent forward rolls

common_errors.error: Releasing cross-body pressure prematurely when attempting back take
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes during transition, recovering guard or achieving standing position
common_errors.correction: Maintain heavy shoulder pressure throughout entire transition sequence, only releasing when hooks are fully secured

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's near-side arm or hip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses free limbs to create frames, stand up, or rotate away from control
common_errors.correction: Establish and maintain hook or grip on near-side arm or hip before attempting transitions, preventing opponent mobility

common_errors.error: Positioning hips too close to opponent allowing easy reversal
common_errors.consequence: Opponent rolls through or reverses position, potentially achieving top position
common_errors.correction: Keep hips back and to the side, maintaining perpendicular angle with mobility to follow opponent's movements

common_errors.error: Overcommitting to one side without adjusting to opponent's direction
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes to opposite side or reverses position using top player's committed weight
common_errors.correction: Stay mobile and ready to switch sides, following opponent's movement rather than forcing predetermined sequences

expert_insights.danaher: The cross body ride represents a critical control point in the systematic approach to back attacks. The position's effectiveness lies in its geometric superiority - by establishing a perpendicular angle to the opponent's spine, you create mechanical disadvantage for all their escape attempts while maintaining multiple pathways to dominant positions. The key technical element is understanding weight distribution: your pressure must be directed through the shoulder into the opponent's scapula and thoracic spine, collapsing their turtle structure while your hips remain mobile and positioned away from reversal attempts. This position exemplifies the principle of asymmetric control where minimal energy expenditure on your part requires maximum defensive effort from the opponent. When executing transitions from cross body ride, maintain continuous pressure throughout - the most common technical failure is releasing control pressure before securing the next position. The cross body ride should be viewed not as a static position but as a dynamic control state from which multiple finishing sequences can be initiated based on the opponent's defensive reactions.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the cross body ride is one of my highest-percentage positions for securing back takes against elite opponents. What makes this position so effective at the highest levels is that it puts your opponent in a position where all their escape options lead directly into your offensive sequences. When I establish cross body ride, I'm immediately thinking about the back take, but I'm also ready to capitalize on the crucifix if they post their arm or transition to mount if they flatten out. The competition reality is that turtle is still a common defensive position even at black belt, so being dominant from cross body ride is essential for any serious competitor. My approach emphasizes staying heavy but mobile - you need to make them carry your weight but be ready to flow with their escape attempts rather than fighting them. Against high-level opponents, I've found the most success comes from using the cross body ride to exhaust their defensive energy before finishing the back take, rather than rushing the transition. The position also sets up my favorite submissions - once I transition to back control from here, the finishing rate on the rear naked choke or bow and arrow is extremely high because the opponent is already compromised from defending the ride.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The cross body ride in the 10th Planet system is all about setting up the truck position and twister, but it's also a sick position for straight-up back takes. What people don't realize is how dynamic you can be from this position - you're not just holding them down, you're constantly hunting for the submission or the next position upgrade. One of my favorite sequences is using the cross body ride to bait the opponent into trying to roll, then catching them mid-roll and taking the back or hitting the crab ride. The key is staying loose and ready to flow with their movement rather than being static and heavy. We drill a lot of situations where the bottom guy is trying everything to escape and you're just flowing from cross body to truck to twister to back control. The beauty of the position is that it's low-risk, high-reward - even if they start to escape, you're in a great position to follow them and end up in an even better spot. For no-gi, this position is absolutely essential because without the gi grips, controlling turtle requires this kind of dynamic, body-weight-based control. I teach my students to think of the cross body ride as a launching pad for all the crazy shit we do from turtle - it's the position that makes everything else possible.
